claim: Natural killer (NK) cells can control metastasis through cytotoxicity and IFN-γ production independently of T cells in experimental metastasis mouse models.
source: Natural killer (NK) cells can control metastasis through cytotoxicity and IFN-γ production independently of T cells in experimental metastasis mouse models.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work establishing this mechanism.

claim: The inverse correlation between NK activity and metastasis incidence supports a critical role for NK cells in human metastatic surveillance.
source: The inverse correlation between NK activity and metastasis incidence supports a critical role for NK cells in human metastatic surveillance.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about NK cell function in humans.

claim: Autologous NK cell therapy has shown limited benefit in treating patients with metastatic solid tumors.
source: However, autologous NK cell therapy has shown limited benefit in treating patients with metastatic solid tumors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: Transfer of IL-15/IL-12-conditioned syngeneic NK cells after primary tumor resection promoted long-term survival of mice with low metastatic burden.
source: Using a spontaneous metastasis mouse model of MHC-I+ breast cancer, we found that transfer of IL-15/IL-12-conditioned syngeneic NK cells after primary tumor resection promoted long-term survival of mice with low metastatic burden
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the mouse model presented in the manuscript.

claim: NK cell therapy induced a tumor-specific protective T cell response that is essential for the therapeutic effect.
source: we found that transfer of IL-15/IL-12-conditioned syngeneic NK cells after primary tumor resection promoted long-term survival of mice with low metastatic burden and induced a tumor-specific protective T cell response that is essential for the therapeutic effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from T cell depletion and adoptive transfer experiments.

claim: NK cell transfer augments activation of conventional dendritic cells (cDCs), Foxp3-CD4+ T cells and stem cell-like CD8+ T cells in metastatic lungs.
source: Furthermore, NK cell transfer augments activation of conventional dendritic cells (cDCs), Foxp3-CD4+ T cells and stem cell-like CD8+ T cells in metastatic lungs
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: IFN-γ of the transferred NK cells contributes significantly to the augmented activation of cDCs and T cells in metastatic lungs.
source: Furthermore, NK cell transfer augments activation of conventional dendritic cells (cDCs), Foxp3-CD4+ T cells and stem cell-like CD8+ T cells in metastatic lungs, to which IFN-γ of the transferred NK cells contributes significantly.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments using Ifng-/- NK cells showing reduced effects.

claim: Direct interactions between transferred NK cells and endogenous cDCs enhance T cell activation.
source: These results imply direct interactions between transferred NK cells and endogenous cDCs to enhance T cell activation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the requirement for IFN-γ from transferred NK cells and the observed cDC activation.

claim: Autologous NK cell therapy was safe in six patients with advanced cancer.
source: We conducted an investigator-initiated clinical trial of autologous NK cell therapy in six patients with advanced cancer and observed that the NK cell therapy was safe and showed signs of effectiveness.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical trial data showing no treatment-related adverse effects.

claim: Autologous NK cell therapy showed signs of effectiveness in six patients with advanced cancer.
source: We conducted an investigator-initiated clinical trial of autologous NK cell therapy in six patients with advanced cancer and observed that the NK cell therapy was safe and showed signs of effectiveness.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical response data showing stable disease and survival outcomes.

claim: Autologous NK cell therapy is effective in treating established low burden metastases of MHC-I+ tumor cells by activating the cDC-T cell axis at metastatic sites.
source: These findings indicate that autologous NK cell therapy is effective in treating established low burden metastases of MHC-I+ tumor cells by activating the cDC-T cell axis at metastatic sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined mouse model data and clinical trial results.

claim: Metastasis is the most common cause of cancer death.
source: Metastasis is the most common cause of cancer death, and effective therapies for established metastases are currently lacking (Ganesh and Massagué, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Effective therapies for established metastases are currently lacking.
source: Metastasis is the most common cause of cancer death, and effective therapies for established metastases are currently lacking (Ganesh and Massagué, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The abundance of functional circulating or tumor-infiltrating NK cells is inversely correlated with metastasis incidence.
source: Natural killer (NK) cells play a critical role in metastasis control, as the abundance of functional circulating or tumor-infiltrating NK cells is inversely correlated with metastasis incidence while being positively correlated with favorable prognoses for patients with or at risk of metastasis (López-Soto et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The abundance of functional circulating or tumor-infiltrating NK cells is positively correlated with favorable prognoses for patients with or at risk of metastasis.
source: Natural killer (NK) cells play a critical role in metastasis control, as the abundance of functional circulating or tumor-infiltrating NK cells is inversely correlated with metastasis incidence while being positively correlated with favorable prognoses for patients with or at risk of metastasis (López-Soto et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: NK cells are capable of recognizing tumor cells via various activating and inhibitory NK receptors (NKRs).
source: NK cells are capable of recognizing tumor cells via various activating and inhibitory NK receptors (NKRs).
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about NK cell biology.

claim: Tumor cells often down-regulate the expression of ligands for inhibitory NKRs, yet express stress-induced ligands for activating NKRs.
source: Tumor cells often down-regulate the expression of ligands for inhibitory NKRs, yet express stress-induced ligands for activating NKRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about tumor cell immune evasion.

claim: Reduced inhibitory NKR engagement and enhanced activating NKR engagement facilitate NK cell activation upon encountering tumor cells.
source: Upon encountering tumor cells, the reduced inhibitory NKR engagement and enhanced activating NKR engagement facilitate NK cell activation (Jamieson et al., 2002; Kärre et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NK cells express receptors for activating cytokines, such as IL-15, IL-12, IL-18, and IL-21.
source: NK cells also express receptors for activating cytokines, such as IL-15, IL-12, IL-18, and IL-21, as well as receptors for suppressive factors such as TGF-β and prostaglandin E2 present in the tumor microenvironment (Huntington et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: NK cells express receptors for suppressive factors such as TGF-β and prostaglandin E2 present in the tumor microenvironment.
source: NK cells also express receptors for activating cytokines, such as IL-15, IL-12, IL-18, and IL-21, as well as receptors for suppressive factors such as TGF-β and prostaglandin E2 present in the tumor microenvironment (Huntington et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The sum of signals transduced through the activating and inhibitory receptors determines NK cell activation.
source: The sum of signals transduced through the activating and inhibitory receptors determines NK cell activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about NK cell signaling.

claim: Activated NK cells kill engaged tumor cells via perforin, granzymes, and the death receptor ligands TNF-α, TRAIL, and FasL.
source: Activated NK cells kill engaged tumor cells via perforin, granzymes, and the death receptor ligands TNF-α, TRAIL, and FasL (Smyth et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Activated NK cells produce IFN-γ, which directly inhibits tumor cell growth.
source: Activated NK cells also produce IFN-γ, which directly inhibits tumor cell growth and induces type 1 T helper cell (TH1) and cytotoxic CD8+ T cell responses that are critical for effective anti-tumor immunity (Alspach et al., 2019; Martín Fontecha et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IFN-γ produced by activated NK cells induces type 1 T helper cell (TH1) and cytotoxic CD8+ T cell responses that are critical for effective anti-tumor immunity.
source: Activated NK cells also produce IFN-γ, which directly inhibits tumor cell growth and induces type 1 T helper cell (TH1) and cytotoxic CD8+ T cell responses that are critical for effective anti-tumor immunity (Alspach et al., 2019; Martín Fontecha et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Intratumoral NK cells produce XCL1 and CCL5 to recruit type 1 conventional dendritic cells (cDC1) that cross-present cell-associated tumor antigen to CD8+ T cells.
source: Moreover, intratumoral NK cells produce XCL1 and CCL5 to recruit type 1 conventional dendritic cells (cDC1) that cross-present cell-associated tumor antigen to CD8+ T cells (Böttcher et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Intratumoral NK cells produce Flt3L to increase the abundance of cDCs.
source: and also produce Flt3L to increase the abundance of cDCs (Barry et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The immunosuppressive microenvironment induced by tumor cells elicits NK cell and T cell dysfunction.
source: However, the immunosuppressive microenvironment induced by tumor cells elicits NK cell and T cell dysfunction (Melaiu et al., 2019; Thommen and Schumacher, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Two anti-metastatic mechanisms of NK cells have been revealed to date: cytotoxicity and IFN-γ production.
source: Two anti-metastatic mechanisms of NK cells have been revealed to date, i.e., cytotoxicity and IFN-γ production.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The epithelial-mesenchymal transition increases the susceptibility of tumor cells to NK cell cytotoxicity by modulating the expression of ligands for the activating NKRs NKG2D.
source: In the metastatic cascade, the epithelial-mesenchymal transition increases the susceptibility of tumor cells to NK cell cytotoxicity by modulating the expression of ligands for the activating NKRs NKG2D (López-Soto et al., 2013), E-cadherin and cell adhesion molecule 1 (Chockley et al., 2018), as well as MHC class I (MHC-I) molecules (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The epithelial-mesenchymal transition increases the susceptibility of tumor cells to NK cell cytotoxicity by modulating the expression of E-cadherin and cell adhesion molecule 1.
source: In the metastatic cascade, the epithelial-mesenchymal transition increases the susceptibility of tumor cells to NK cell cytotoxicity by modulating the expression of ligands for the activating NKRs NKG2D (López-Soto et al., 2013), E-cadherin and cell adhesion molecule 1 (Chockley et al., 2018), as well as MHC class I (MHC-I) molecules (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The epithelial-mesenchymal transition increases the susceptibility of tumor cells to NK cell cytotoxicity by modulating the expression of MHC class I (MHC-I) molecules.
source: In the metastatic cascade, the epithelial-mesenchymal transition increases the susceptibility of tumor cells to NK cell cytotoxicity by modulating the expression of ligands for the activating NKRs NKG2D (López-Soto et al., 2013), E-cadherin and cell adhesion molecule 1 (Chockley et al., 2018), as well as MHC class I (MHC-I) molecules (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IFN-γ produced by NK cells is essential for natural resistance to lung metastasis in a B16 melanoma model using Rag knockout mice that lacked T cells.
source: The IFN-γ produced by NK cells was shown to be essential for natural resistance to lung metastasis in a B16 melanoma model (Takeda et al., 2011) and for the IL-12-mediated suppression of liver metastasis in a CT-26 model (Uemura et al., 2010) using Rag knockout mice that lacked T cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IFN-γ produced by NK cells is essential for the IL-12-mediated suppression of liver metastasis in a CT-26 model using Rag knockout mice that lacked T cells.
source: The IFN-γ produced by NK cells was shown to be essential for natural resistance to lung metastasis in a B16 melanoma model (Takeda et al., 2011) and for the IL-12-mediated suppression of liver metastasis in a CT-26 model (Uemura et al., 2010) using Rag knockout mice that lacked T cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The anti-metastasis effect of IL-12 produced by Batf3-dependent DCs is mediated through IFN-γ production by NK cells without the involvement of T cells.
source: Another study indicated that the anti-metastasis effect of IL-12 produced by Baft3-dependent DCs is mediated through IFN-γ production by NK cells without the involvement of T cells (Mittal et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: NK cells sustain the dormancy of metastatic tumor cells seeded in distal organs through cytotoxicity and IFN-γ.
source: NK cells also sustain the dormancy of metastatic tumor cells seeded in distal organs through cytotoxicity and IFN-γ (Correia et al., 2021; Malladi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Adoptive transfer of ex vivo-expanded autologous NK cells has shown limited clinical benefit in treating patients with metastatic or locally advanced solid tumors, including melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, and digestive cancer.
source: Despite the clear anti-tumor function of endogenous NK cells, adoptive transfer of ex vivo-expanded autologous NK cells has shown limited clinical benefit in treating patients with metastatic or locally advanced solid tumors, including melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, and digestive cancer (Parkhurst et al., 2011; Sakamoto et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: The immunosuppressive microenvironment induced by tumor cells likely contributes to the therapeutic limitation of autologous NK cell therapy.
source: Both the immunosuppressive microenvironment induced by tumor cells (Melaiu et al., 2019) and heterogeneity of NK cell subpopulations and their respective functions (Freud et al., 2017) likely contribute to this therapeutic limitation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and represents speculation about mechanisms.

claim: Heterogeneity of NK cell subpopulations and their respective functions likely contributes to the therapeutic limitation of autologous NK cell therapy.
source: Both the immunosuppressive microenvironment induced by tumor cells (Melaiu et al., 2019) and heterogeneity of NK cell subpopulations and their respective functions (Freud et al., 2017) likely contribute to this therapeutic limitation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and represents speculation about mechanisms.

claim: On average, 86% of the IL-15/IL-12-cultured cells were identified as TCRαβ-TCRγδ-CD19-NK1.1+ that express NKG2D, EOMES and T-bet.
source: On average, 86% of the resulting cells were identified as TCRαβ-TCRγδ-CD19-NK1.1+ that express NKG2D, EOMES and T-bet (Figure 1A), representing characteristics of NK cells (Gordon et al., 2012; Raulet, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Approximately 90% of the expanded NK cells were CD27+ with no-to-low levels of CD11b expression.
source: Approximately 90% of the expanded NK cells were CD27+ with no-to-low levels of CD11b expression (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The proportion of NK cells expressing MHC-I-interacting NKRs, including activating Ly49D/H and inhibitory Ly49A/G2/I and NKG2A, was stable among independent cultures.
source: The proportion of NK cells expressing MHC-I-interacting NKRs, including activating Ly49D/H and inhibitory Ly49A/G2/I and NKG2A, was stable among independent cultures (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: On average, 87% of the expanded NK cells expressed either intermediate or high levels of the activating receptor DNAM-1.
source: In terms of activation status, on average, 87% of the expanded NK cells expressed either intermediate or high levels of the activating receptor DNAM-1 and 82% of them displayed an activated B220+CD11c+ phenotype (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 82% of the expanded NK cells displayed an activated B220+CD11c+ phenotype.
source: In terms of activation status, on average, 87% of the expanded NK cells expressed either intermediate or high levels of the activating receptor DNAM-1 and 82% of them displayed an activated B220+CD11c+ phenotype (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The expanded NK cells expressed the anti-tumor effectors IFN-γ, granzyme B, and TRAIL.
source: Consistently, they expressed the anti-tumor effectors IFN-γ, granzyme B, and TRAIL (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Co-culturing the NK cells with either EO771 breast adenocarcinoma cells or B16F10 melanoma cells in vitro resulted in dose-dependent tumor cell death.
source: Co-culturing the NK cells with either EO771 breast adenocarcinoma cells that express MHC-I molecules and Rae-1 or B16F10 melanoma cells that express none of those molecules in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) resulted in dose-dependent tumor cell death (Figure 1E)
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Co-culturing the NK cells with either EO771 or B16F10 tumor cells resulted in up-regulation of IFN-γ production by the NK cells.
source: Co-culturing the NK cells with either EO771 breast adenocarcinoma cells that express MHC-I molecules and Rae-1 or B16F10 melanoma cells that express none of those molecules in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) resulted in dose-dependent tumor cell death (Figure 1E) and up-regulation of IFN-γ production by the NK cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: EO771 cells express MHC-I molecules and Rae-1.
source: Co-culturing the NK cells with either EO771 breast adenocarcinoma cells that express MHC-I molecules and Rae-1 or B16F10 melanoma cells that express none of those molecules in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: B16F10 melanoma cells express none of MHC-I molecules or Rae-1.
source: Co-culturing the NK cells with either EO771 breast adenocarcinoma cells that express MHC-I molecules and Rae-1 or B16F10 melanoma cells that express none of those molecules in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The NK cells conditioned by means of IL-15 and IL-12 possess anti-tumor activities in vitro.
source: Thus, the NK cells conditioned by means of IL-15 and IL-12 possess anti-tumor activities in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by the in vitro cytotoxicity and IFN-γ production data.

claim: At 21 days post-inoculation, ~85% of mice with a primary tumor weighing ≥95 mg had metastatic foci on the lung surface.
source: At 21 days post-inoculation and consistent with the spontaneous lung metastatic property of the EO771 line (Ewens et al., 2005), we observed that ~85% of mice with a primary tumor weighing ≥95 mg had metastatic foci on the lung surface.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations in the mouse model.

claim: The number and area of metastatic foci was positively correlated with tumor weight on day 21.
source: The number and area of metastatic foci was positively correlated with tumor weight on day 21 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Resection of the primary tumor and its sentinel lymph node (LN) on day 21 resulted in a long-term survival rate of 18%.
source: Resection of the primary tumor and its sentinel lymph node (LN) on day 21 resulted in a long-term survival rate of 18%, with mortality of all remaining mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: All dead mice after tumor resection exhibited metastases in the lung.
source: All dead mice exhibited metastases in the lung, of which 71% displayed tumor reappearance at the surgical site (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: 71% of dead mice after tumor resection displayed tumor reappearance at the surgical site.
source: All dead mice exhibited metastases in the lung, of which 71% displayed tumor reappearance at the surgical site (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: The tumor resection model represents a model of established metastases caused by tumor cell dissemination before and arising from surgery.
source: Therefore, this tumor resection model represents a model of established metastases caused by tumor cell dissemination before and arising from surgery.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of metastases in resected mice.

claim: The expanded NK cells express the chemokine receptors CXCR3, CCR5, and CXCR6.
source: The expanded NK cells express the chemokine receptors CXCR3, CCR5, and CXCR6 (Figure 2C)
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The lung of tumor-resected mice express mRNA of the chemokine ligands CXCL9/10/11, CCL3/4/5, and CXCL16.
source: and the lung of tumor-resected mice express mRNA of the corresponding ligands CXCL9/10/11, CCL3/4/5, and CXCL16 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Numbers of transferred eGFP+ NK cells in the lung peaked at 4 hr and then continuously declined, remaining detectable for at least 2 days.
source: Using eGFP+ NK cells, we observed that numbers of transferred cells in the lung peaked at 4 hr and then continuously declined, remaining detectable for at least 2 days (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: A similar pattern of transferred NK cells was observed in the spleen, albeit with lower cell counts.
source: A similar pattern of transferred NK cells was observed in the spleen, albeit with lower cell counts (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: There is a negative correlation between survival time and day 21 tumor weight in the NK-cell-treated group.
source: We evaluated the effect of syngeneic NK cell therapy on tumor-resected mice (Figure 3A Schema), and found a negative correlation between survival time and day 21 tumor weight in the NK-cell-treated group but not in the control group (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There is no correlation between survival time and day 21 tumor weight in the control group.
source: We evaluated the effect of syngeneic NK cell therapy on tumor-resected mice (Figure 3A Schema), and found a negative correlation between survival time and day 21 tumor weight in the NK-cell-treated group but not in the control group (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: NK-cell-treated mice displayed significantly enhanced overall survival (OS) and an improved long-term survival rate from 33% to 68% compared to control mice in the 95–400 mg tumor group.
source: NK-cell-treated mice displayed significantly enhanced overall survival (OS) and an improved long-term survival rate from 33% to 68% compared to control mice in the 95–400 mg tumor group, whereas the same therapy did not improve OS of the >400 mg tumor group (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: NK cell therapy did not improve OS of the >400 mg tumor group.
source: NK-cell-treated mice displayed significantly enhanced overall survival (OS) and an improved long-term survival rate from 33% to 68% compared to control mice in the 95–400 mg tumor group, whereas the same therapy did not improve OS of the >400 mg tumor group (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The NK cell therapy promotes long-term survival of tumor-resected mice carrying low metastatic burden.
source: These results, together with the result presented in Figure 2A, indicate that the NK cell therapy promotes long-term survival of tumor-resected mice carrying low metastatic burden.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between tumor weight and metastatic burden, and the survival benefit in low tumor weight mice.

claim: 83% of surviving mice after NK cell treatment were protected from EO771 re-challenge and survived beyond 180 days.
source: We found that 83% of these mice were protected from EO771 re-challenge and survived beyond 180 days, whereas all mice re-challenged with B16F10 died (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: All surviving mice after NK cell treatment that were re-challenged with B16F10 died.
source: We found that 83% of these mice were protected from EO771 re-challenge and survived beyond 180 days, whereas all mice re-challenged with B16F10 died (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Age-matched naïve mice inoculated for the first time with either EO771 or B16F10 all died.
source: Age-matched naïve mice inoculated for the first time with either EO771 or B16F10 as a control all died (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Surviving mice of post-resection NK cell therapy displayed tumor-specific protective immunity.
source: Thus, surviving mice of post-resection NK cell therapy displayed tumor-specific protective immunity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the protection against EO771 but not B16F10 re-challenge.

claim: In the 95–600 mg tumor group, depletion of CD8+ cells alone or both CD4+ and CD8+ cells diminished the effect of NK cell therapy.
source: In the 95–600 mg tumor group, depletion of CD8+ cells alone or both CD4+ and CD8+ cells diminished the effect of NK cell therapy, whereas depletion of CD4+ cells alone did not affect OS (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis with T cell depletion shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In the 95–600 mg tumor group, depletion of CD4+ cells alone did not affect OS.
source: In the 95–600 mg tumor group, depletion of CD8+ cells alone or both CD4+ and CD8+ cells diminished the effect of NK cell therapy, whereas depletion of CD4+ cells alone did not affect OS (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis with T cell depletion shown in Figure 3D.

claim: CD8+ T cells are essential for the effect of NK cell therapy.
source: This result indicates that CD8+ T cells are essential for the effect of NK cell therapy.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the loss of therapeutic effect upon CD8+ T cell depletion.

claim: The >600 mg tumor group displayed a limited NK cell treatment effect but did exhibit an improvement in OS upon depleting CD4+ cells alone.
source: In contrast, the >600 mg tumor group displayed a limited NK cell treatment effect as expected, but did exhibit an improvement in OS upon depleting CD4+ cells alone (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The proportion of lung Foxp3+CD4+ T cells in CD45+ cells positively correlated with day 21 tumor weight.
source: As the proportion of lung Foxp3+CD4+ T cells in CD45+ cells positively correlated with day 21 tumor weight (data not shown), depletion of Foxp3+CD4+ T cells by anti-CD4 antibody likely has a stronger effect in augmenting the immune response for the >600 mg tumor than the 95–600 mg tumor group.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Depletion of Foxp3+CD4+ T cells by anti-CD4 antibody likely has a stronger effect in augmenting the immune response for the >600 mg tumor than the 95–600 mg tumor group.
source: As the proportion of lung Foxp3+CD4+ T cells in CD45+ cells positively correlated with day 21 tumor weight (data not shown), depletion of Foxp3+CD4+ T cells by anti-CD4 antibody likely has a stronger effect in augmenting the immune response for the >600 mg tumor than the 95–600 mg tumor group.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the correlation between Foxp3+CD4+ T cells and tumor weight.

claim: Both tumor groups showed diminished OS upon depletion of both CD4+ and CD8+ cells than was the case for depletion of CD8+ cells alone, indicating a CD8+ T cell-independent anti-tumor effect of CD4+ T cells.
source: Moreover, both tumor groups showed diminished OS upon depletion of both CD4+ and CD8+ cells than was the case for depletion of CD8+ cells alone, indicating a CD8+ T cell-independent anti-tumor effect of CD4+ T cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of survival outcomes with different T cell depletion strategies.

claim: 5 of 6 T-cell recipients from NK cell-treated and EO771-rechallenged survivors survived beyond 120 days post tumor inoculation.
source: For the mice receiving cells isolated from the survivors, 5 of 6 T-cell recipients and 1 of 6 non-T-cell recipients survived beyond 120 days post tumor inoculation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: 1 of 6 non-T-cell recipients from NK cell-treated and EO771-rechallenged survivors survived beyond 120 days post tumor inoculation.
source: For the mice receiving cells isolated from the survivors, 5 of 6 T-cell recipients and 1 of 6 non-T-cell recipients survived beyond 120 days post tumor inoculation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Mice receiving either T or non-T cells isolated from age-matched naive donors all died.
source: In contrast, mice receiving either T or non-T cells isolated from age-matched naive donors all died.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data.

claim: The post-resection NK cell therapy induces a tumor-specific T cell response with memory that is essential for its treatment efficacy.
source: Together, these results indicate that the post-resection NK cell therapy induces a tumor-specific T cell response with memory that is essential for its treatment efficacy.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the adoptive transfer experiments showing T cells from survivors confer anti-tumor activity.

claim: Lung cDC1s and cDC2s consist of cells expressing either high or low level of MHC-II (MHC-IIhi or MHC-IIlo).
source: We found that lung cDC1s and cDC2s consist of cells expressing either high or low level of MHC-II (MHC-IIhi or MHC-IIlo), and the MHC-IIhi cDCs are composed of CCR7+Lamp3+ and CCR7-Lamp3- subsets (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The MHC-IIhi cDCs are composed of CCR7+Lamp3+ and CCR7-Lamp3- subsets.
source: We found that lung cDC1s and cDC2s consist of cells expressing either high or low level of MHC-II (MHC-IIhi or MHC-IIlo), and the MHC-IIhi cDCs are composed of CCR7+Lamp3+ and CCR7-Lamp3- subsets (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The CCR7+Lamp3+MHC-IIhi subset expresses the highest level of APC function molecules, including MHC-I, MHC-II, CCR7, CD86, CD40, and PD-L1.
source: The CCR7+Lamp3+MHC-IIhi subset expresses the highest level of APC function molecules, including MHC-I, MHC-II, CCR7, CD86, CD40, and PD-L1 (Figure 4A), resembling the recently identified mregDC (Cheng et al., 2021; de Saint-Vis et al., 1998; Maier et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The CCR7+Lamp3+MHC-IIhi subset resembles the recently identified mregDC.
source: The CCR7+Lamp3+MHC-IIhi subset expresses the highest level of APC function molecules, including MHC-I, MHC-II, CCR7, CD86, CD40, and PD-L1 (Figure 4A), resembling the recently identified mregDC (Cheng et al., 2021; de Saint-Vis et al., 1998; Maier et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the phenotypic similarity to mregDCs described in cited literature.

claim: Transfer of WT NK cells significantly increased the proportion of the two MHC-IIhi subsets among cDC1s.
source: However, among cDC1s, transfer of WT NK cells significantly increased the proportion of the two MHC-IIhi subsets, the levels of CD86 and CD40 expressed by all three subsets, and the levels of PD-L1, MHC-I and MHC-II expressed by CCR7-Lamp3-MHC-IIhi and MHC-IIlo subsets (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Transfer of WT NK cells increased the levels of CD86 and CD40 expressed by all three cDC1 subsets.
source: However, among cDC1s, transfer of WT NK cells significantly increased the proportion of the two MHC-IIhi subsets, the levels of CD86 and CD40 expressed by all three subsets, and the levels of PD-L1, MHC-I and MHC-II expressed by CCR7-Lamp3-MHC-IIhi and MHC-IIlo subsets (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Transfer of WT NK cells increased the levels of PD-L1, MHC-I and MHC-II expressed by CCR7-Lamp3-MHC-IIhi and MHC-IIlo cDC1 subsets.
source: However, among cDC1s, transfer of WT NK cells significantly increased the proportion of the two MHC-IIhi subsets, the levels of CD86 and CD40 expressed by all three subsets, and the levels of PD-L1, MHC-I and MHC-II expressed by CCR7-Lamp3-MHC-IIhi and MHC-IIlo subsets (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: IFN-γ, but not IL-10, of the transferred NK cells significantly contributes to the effects on cDC1s, except for the PD-L1 level in MHC-IIlo subset.
source: IFN-γ, but not IL-10, of the transferred NK cells significantly contributes to these effects, except for the PD-L1 level in MHC-IIlo subset (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of WT, Il10-/-, and Ifng-/- NK cell effects shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Transfer of WT NK cells exerted many effects on cDC2s similar to those described for cDC1s, albeit with several differences.
source: Transfer of WT NK cells exerted many effects on cDC2s similar to those described above for cDC1s, albeit with several differences (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Transfer of WT NK cells augmented MHC-II level in the CCR7+Lamp3+MHC-IIhi cDC2 subset.
source: The differences include augmenting MHC-II level in the CCR7+Lamp3+MHC-IIhi subset, reducing MHC-II level in the MHC-IIlo subset, and having no effect on CD40 level in the CCR7+Lamp3+MHC-IIhi subset (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Transfer of WT NK cells reduced MHC-II level in the MHC-IIlo cDC2 subset.
source: The differences include augmenting MHC-II level in the CCR7+Lamp3+MHC-IIhi subset, reducing MHC-II level in the MHC-IIlo subset, and having no effect on CD40 level in the CCR7+Lamp3+MHC-IIhi subset (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Transfer of WT NK cells had no effect on CD40 level in the CCR7+Lamp3+MHC-IIhi cDC2 subset.
source: The differences include augmenting MHC-II level in the CCR7+Lamp3+MHC-IIhi subset, reducing MHC-II level in the MHC-IIlo subset, and having no effect on CD40 level in the CCR7+Lamp3+MHC-IIhi subset (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Transfer of WT NK cells increased the proportion of Foxp3-CD4+ and CD8+ T cells without altering that of Foxp3+CD4+ T cells.
source: Transfer of WT NK cells increased the proportion of Foxp3-CD4+ and CD8+ T cells without altering that of Foxp3+CD4+ T cells (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The proportion of activated Foxp3-CD4+ T cells, including effector (CD62L-CD44+), PD-1+ and Ki67+ subsets, increased upon transfer of WT NK cells.
source: The proportion of activated Foxp3-CD4+ T cells, including effector (CD62L-CD44+), PD-1+ and Ki67+ subsets, also increased (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: These effects on Foxp3-CD4+ T cells were not observed for mice that received Ifng-/- NK cells.
source: These effects were not observed for mice that received Ifng-/- NK cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Transfer of Il10-/-, but not WT, NK cells increased the proportion of CD62L+CD44+ and CD62L-CD44+ subsets in PD-1-Lag3- CD8+ T cells.
source: We reasoned that PD-1-Lag3- CD8+ T cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) are either naïve or at a very early stage of activation, and found that transfer of Il10-/-, but not WT, NK cells increased the proportion of CD62L+CD44+ and CD62L-CD44+ subsets, while the proportion of CD62L-CD44+ and Ki67+ subsets were lower in mice that received Ifng-/- NK cells compared to those in mice that received WT NK cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The proportion of CD62L-CD44+ and Ki67+ subsets in PD-1-Lag3- CD8+ T cells were lower in mice that received Ifng-/- NK cells compared to those in mice that received WT NK cells.
source: We reasoned that PD-1-Lag3- CD8+ T cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) are either naïve or at a very early stage of activation, and found that transfer of Il10-/-, but not WT, NK cells increased the proportion of CD62L+CD44+ and CD62L-CD44+ subsets, while the proportion of CD62L-CD44+ and Ki67+ subsets were lower in mice that received Ifng-/- NK cells compared to those in mice that received WT NK cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: IL-10 of transferred NK cells inhibits activation of naive CD8+ T cells.
source: These results indicate that IL-10 of transferred NK cells inhibits activation of naive CD8+ T cells, whereas IFN-γ of transferred NK cells promotes their effector differentiation and proliferation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the increased activation in Il10-/- NK cell recipients.

claim: IFN-γ of transferred NK cells promotes effector differentiation and proliferation of naive CD8+ T cells.
source: These results indicate that IL-10 of transferred NK cells inhibits activation of naive CD8+ T cells, whereas IFN-γ of transferred NK cells promotes their effector differentiation and proliferation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the decreased activation in Ifng-/- NK cell recipients.

claim: Transfer of WT or Il10-/-, but not Ifng-/-, NK cells increased total and Ki67+ SCL CD8+ T cells.
source: We further examined stem cell-like (SCL) CD8+ T cells that are Tim3- in PD-1loLag3- CD8+ cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; Castiglioni et al., 2023), and detected an increase of total and Ki67+ SCL CD8+ T cells in mice that received WT or Il10-/-, but not Ifng-/-, NK cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Transfer of Il10-/- NK cells resulted in a higher level of SCL CD8+ T cells than when WT NK cells were transferred.
source: Transfer of Il10-/- NK cells resulted in a higher level of SCL CD8+ T cells than when WT NK cells were transferred (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: NK cell transfer did not alter the proportion of exhausted or PEX CD8+ T cells.
source: In contrast, NK cell transfer did not alter the proportion of exhausted or PEX CD8+ T cells (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Transfer of the IL-15/IL-12-conditioned syngeneic NK cells augmented the activation of cDC1s and cDC2s, as well as the levels and activation of Foxp3-CD4+ T cells, naïve CD8+ T cells and SCL CD8+ T cells in metastatic lungs.
source: Thus, overall, transfer of the IL-15/IL-12-conditioned syngeneic NK cells augmented the activation of cDC1s and cDC2s, as well as the levels and activation of Foxp3-CD4+ T cells, naïve CD8+ T cells and SCL CD8+ T cells in metastatic lungs.
evidence: This claim summarizes the findings from Figures 4 and 5.

claim: >90% of migratory cDC1s and >65% of migratory cDC2s express CCR7 and LAMP3.
source: We analyzed migratory and resident cDCs in mLN (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), and found that >90% of migratory cDC1s and >65% of migratory cDC2s express CCR7 and LAMP3 (Figure 6A), a phenotype similar to lung CCR7+LAMP3+MHC-IIhi cDC1 and cDC2.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The great majority of resident cDC1s and cDC2s in mLN are CCR7-LAMP3-.
source: On the other hand, the great majority of resident cDC1s and cDC2s in mLN are CCR7-LAMP3- (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Transfer of WT NK cells increased the proportion of migratory cDC1 in cDCs and the level of CD86 expression by both migratory cDC1s and cDC2s, which required IFN-γ of the transferred NK cells.
source: Transfer of WT NK cells increased the proportion of migratory cDC1 in cDCs and the level of CD86 expression by both migratory cDC1s and cDC2s, which required IFN-γ of the transferred NK cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: NK cell transfer did not affect the proportion or activation of Foxp3-CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in mLN.
source: We also examined T cells in mLN and found that NK cell transfer affected neither the proportion nor the activation marked by CD44+ or KI67+ of Foxp3-CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (data not show).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: NK cell transfer increased the level of migratory cDC1 and CD86 expression by migratory cDC1s and cDC2s, but did not affect T cell activation in mLN.
source: Collectively, NK cell transfer increased the level of migratory cDC1 and CD86 expression by migratory cDC1s and cDC2s, but did not affect T cell activation in mLN.
evidence: This claim summarizes the findings about mLN.

claim: The expanded human NK cells are identifiable as CD3-CD19-CD14-CD56+EOMES+, with ~90% of the cells expressing HLA-DR.
source: The expanded NK cells are identifiable as CD3-CD19-CD14-CD56+EOMES+, with ~90% of the cells expressing HLA-DR (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Co-culture of the expanded HLA-DR+ NK cells with K562, THP-1 or U937 tumor cells resulted in dose-dependent tumor cell death.
source: Co-culture of the expanded HLA-DR+ NK cells with K562, THP-1 or U937 tumor cells resulted in dose-dependent tumor cell death (Figure 7B)
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Co-culture of the expanded HLA-DR+ NK cells with K562, THP-1 or U937 tumor cells resulted in increased IFN-γ production by the NK cells.
source: Co-culture of the expanded HLA-DR+ NK cells with K562, THP-1 or U937 tumor cells resulted in dose-dependent tumor cell death (Figure 7B) and increased IFN-γ production by the NK cells (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The patients enrolled in the clinical trial had an ECOG performance status of 0.
source: The patients had an ECOG performance status of 0, a predicted survival of >3 months, and a relatively small target lesion size (6.4–22.7 mm), suggesting relatively low tumor burden.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical trial enrollment criteria and patient characteristics.

claim: The patients enrolled in the clinical trial had a predicted survival of >3 months.
source: The patients had an ECOG performance status of 0, a predicted survival of >3 months, and a relatively small target lesion size (6.4–22.7 mm), suggesting relatively low tumor burden.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical trial enrollment criteria.

claim: The patients enrolled in the clinical trial had a relatively small target lesion size (6.4–22.7 mm), suggesting relatively low tumor burden.
source: The patients had an ECOG performance status of 0, a predicted survival of >3 months, and a relatively small target lesion size (6.4–22.7 mm), suggesting relatively low tumor burden.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical trial patient characteristics and represents inference about tumor burden.

claim: The infused cells were total cells expanded from TCRβ-CD19- PBMCs, of which median 92.4% (83.2–94.9%) were HLA-DR+ NK cells.
source: The infused cells were total cells expanded from TCRβ-CD19- PBMCs, of which median 92.4% (83.2–94.9%) were HLA-DR+ NK cells (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The composition of the infused cells differed slightly among patients, but was stable for each patient over the six infusions.
source: The composition of the infused cells differed slightly among patients, but was stable for each patient over the six infusions (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The expression of NKRs, CD16 and CXCR3 on the HLA-DR+ NK cells was stable for each patient over six batches of cell preparations, apart from some variation in NKp44 for patient 5 and CXCR3 for patient 4.
source: We examined the expression of NKRs, CD16 and CXCR3 on the HLA-DR+ NK cells and determined that it was stable for each patient over six batches of cell preparations, apart from some variation in NKp44 for patient 5 and CXCR3 for patient 4 (Figure 8B, Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The HLA-DR+ NK cells expressed the anti-tumor effectors perforin and IFN-γ.
source: Moreover, the HLA-DR+ NK cells expressed the anti-tumor effectors perforin and IFN-γ (Figure 8C, Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: All patients completed the course of six infusions.
source: All patients completed the course of six infusions.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical trial data.

claim: The therapy proved safe and was well-tolerated by all patients, as no treatment-related adverse effect was observed throughout the entire infusion period up to 24 hr after the final infusion.
source: The therapy proved safe and was well-tolerated by all patients, as no treatment-related adverse effect was observed throughout the entire infusion period up to 24 hr after the final infusion.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical trial safety data.

claim: All patients were in a stable disease (SD) state at month 1.
source: All patients were in a stable disease (SD) state at month 1 (i.e. 1 week after the second infusion), and completed six infusions by month 2.3.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical response data.

claim: Patient 1 exhibited progressive disease (PD) at month 2.7 and left the trial.
source: Patient 1 exhibited progressive disease (PD) at month 2.7 and left the trial.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical response data.

claim: Patient 2 displayed SD for 8.2 months, during which a partial response (PR) was detected at month 4.4.
source: Patient 2 displayed SD for 8.2 months, during which a partial response (PR) was detected at month 4.4.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical response data.

claim: Patient 2 received maintenance metronomic Endoxan starting from month 8.4, and displayed SD or PR for a further 50 months.
source: She then received maintenance metronomic Endoxan starting from month 8.4, and displayed SD or PR for a further 50 months.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical response data.

claim: Patient 3 displayed SD for 52.7 months.
source: Patient 3 displayed SD for 52.7 months.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical response data.

claim: Patient 4 exhibited an SD state for 13 months, received Tarceva during months 14.9–18.6, suffered PD at month 18.6 that prompted receipt of other treatments, and ultimately left the trial at month 31.5.
source: Patient 4 exhibited an SD state for 13 months, received Tarceva during months 14.9–18.6, suffered PD at month 18.6 that prompted receipt of other treatments, and ultimately left the trial at month 31.5.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical response data.

claim: Patient 5 presented SD for 9.9 months, and received metronomic Endoxan during months 7.7–13.5, 28.9–33.0, and 43.6–46.1.
source: Patient 5 presented SD for 9.9 months, and received metronomic Endoxan during months 7.7–13.5, 28.9–33.0, and 43.6–46.1.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical response data.

claim: Patient 6 retained an SD state for 36.3 months.
source: Patient 6 retained an SD state for 36.3 months, and subsequent ultrasound imaging in month 44.5 supports a continuing SD state.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical response data.

claim: Among the four patients with metastatic solid tumors, patients 3 and 6, who only received NK cell therapy, exhibited a SD state and both survived for 60 months.
source: In contrast, patients 3 and 6, who only received NK cell therapy, exhibited a SD state and both survived for 60 months.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical response and survival data.

claim: The two follicular lymphoma patients (patients 2 and 5) who started maintenance Endoxan therapy ~6 months after undergoing the NK-cell therapy have exhibited a SD state and both survived for 60 months.
source: The two follicular lymphoma patients (patients 2 and 5) who started maintenance Endoxan therapy ~6 months after undergoing the NK-cell therapy have exhibited a SD state and both survived for 60 months.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical response and survival data.

claim: These preliminary results suggest some level of effectiveness for the autologous NK cell therapy.
source: These preliminary results suggest some level of effectiveness for the autologous NK cell therapy, supporting the efficacy of our pre-clinical mouse model.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the clinical trial outcomes.

claim: The limited benefit achieved with adoptive autologous NK cell therapy for metastatic solid tumors is paradoxical given the clear anti-tumor functions of endogenous NK cells.
source: The limited benefit achieved with adoptive autologous NK cell therapy for metastatic solid tumors is paradoxical given the clear anti-tumor functions of endogenous NK cells.
evidence: This claim is based on the contrast between known NK cell functions and clinical outcomes.

claim: The T cell dependency of the NK cell therapy in the mouse model indicates that innate mechanisms are not sufficient to support the long-term survival of mice with EO771 metastases.
source: The T cell dependency of the NK cell therapy in our model indicates that innate mechanisms are not sufficient to support the long-term survival of mice with EO771 metastases, which is consistent with the finding from experimental metastasis models that NK cells alone cannot reduce metastases after tumor cells have seeded the target tissue (Spiegel et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the requirement for T cells in the therapeutic effect.

claim: The timeframe adopted for measuring long-term survival covers the period for the innate effect of the transferred NK cells and the effect of a full T cell response with memory.
source: Importantly, the timeframe we adopted for measuring long-term survival covers the period for the innate effect of the transferred NK cells and the effect of a full T cell response with memory.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental design and known kinetics of immune responses.

claim: The CD8+ T cell dependency implies that the transferred NK cells act as an upstream controller for an effective anti-tumor T cell response.
source: The CD8+ T cell dependency implies that the transferred NK cells act as an upstream controller for an effective anti-tumor T cell response, which is in line with a previous study showing that early intratumoral accumulation of IFN-γ-producing endogenous NK cells is required for CD8+ T cell-mediated eradication of Cox-deficient melanoma in immunocompetent wild-type mice (Bonavita et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the T cell dependency and supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The increase of MHC-IIhi cDC subsets and elevated expression of MHC-I, MHC-II and CD86 by lung cDC1s and cDC2s presumably promotes T cell activation.
source: The increase of MHC-IIhi cDC subsets and elevated expression of MHC-I, MHC-II and CD86 by lung cDC1s and cDC2s presumably promotes T cell activation, which is consistent with the increase of activated lung Foxp3-CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on known DC functions and observed T cell activation.

claim: The elevated CD40 expression by cDC1 and CD4+ T cell activation implies cDC1-relayed CD4+ T cell help for CD8+ T cell response in the lung.
source: Moreover, the elevated CD40 expression by cDC1 and CD4+ T cell activation implies cDC1-relayed CD4+ T cell help for CD8+ T cell response in the lung (Ferris et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed changes and supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Intratumoral tumor-specific SCL CD8+ T cells mediate the responses to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade and adoptive T cell immunotherapies.
source: Intratumoral tumor-specific SCL CD8+ T cells are known to mediate the responses to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade and adoptive T cell immunotherapies (Krishna et al., 2020; Siddiqui et al., 2019) and are supplied from a reservoir of precursors in the tumor dLN (Connolly et al., 2021; Schenkel et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Intratumoral tumor-specific SCL CD8+ T cells are supplied from a reservoir of precursors in the tumor dLN.
source: Intratumoral tumor-specific SCL CD8+ T cells are known to mediate the responses to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade and adoptive T cell immunotherapies (Krishna et al., 2020; Siddiqui et al., 2019) and are supplied from a reservoir of precursors in the tumor dLN (Connolly et al., 2021; Schenkel et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: cDC1s in tumor dLN maintain the SCL CD8+ T cell precursor reservoir.
source: As cDC1s in tumor dLN maintain the SCL CD8+ T cell precursor reservoir (Schenkel et al., 2021), the increase of migratory cDC1 in mLN upon NK cell transfer (Figure 6B) likely contribute to the increase of lung SCL CD8+ T cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The increase of migratory cDC1 in mLN upon NK cell transfer likely contributes to the increase of lung SCL CD8+ T cells.
source: As cDC1s in tumor dLN maintain the SCL CD8+ T cell precursor reservoir (Schenkel et al., 2021), the increase of migratory cDC1 in mLN upon NK cell transfer (Figure 6B) likely contribute to the increase of lung SCL CD8+ T cells.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the observed increase in migratory cDC1 and known functions.

claim: The SCL CD8+ T cell precursors are activated by tumor antigens in the tumor dLN and acquire a stem-like state without an effector phenotype.
source: Moreover, a recent study reported that the SCL CD8+ T cell precursors are activated by tumor antigens in the tumor dLN and acquire a stem-like state without an effector phenotype (Prokhnevska et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: After migrating to a tumor, SCL CD8+ T cells differentiate from SCL to an effector state, which requires costimulation by CD80 and CD86 of APC in the TME.
source: After migrating to a tumor, they differentiate from SCL to an effector state, which requires costimulation by CD80 and CD86 of APC in the TME (Prokhnevska et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The findings of augmented CD86 expression by cDCs and increased proliferating SCL CD8+ T cells in response to NK-cell transfer in metastatic lung are in line with the two-step activation of intratumoral SCL CD8+ T cells.
source: Our findings of augmented CD86 expression by cDCs and increased proliferating SCL CD8+ T cells in response to NK-cell transfer in metastatic lung are in line with the two-step activation of intratumoral SCL CD8+ T cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the consistency between the observed results and the known mechanism.

claim: These results demonstrate a clear association between the activation of lung cDCs and T cells in response to NK cell transfer.
source: Together, these results demonstrate a clear association between the activation of lung cDCs and T cells in response to NK cell transfer.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed coordinated changes in cDCs and T cells.

claim: IFN-γ of transferred NK cells is essential for the augmented activation of both cDCs and T cells.
source: Furthermore, IFN-γ of transferred NK cells is essential for the augmented activation of both cDCs and T cells, strengthening evidence for the scenario that NK cells activate cDCs and then cDCs activate T cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments using Ifng-/- NK cells.

claim: The requirement for IFN-γ of transferred NK cells suggests a direct interaction between transferred NK cells and lung cDCs.
source: The requirement for IFN-γ of transferred NK cells also suggests a direct interaction between transferred NK cells and lung cDCs, which is supported by the increase of CCR7+LAMP3+ MHC-IIhi lung cDCs according to a recent study reporting colocalization of LAMP3+ DCs with NK cells in four types of human solid tumor (Tang et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the IFN-γ requirement and supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: NK-cell-derived IFN-γ drives the generation of mregDCs.
source: Moreover, this result indicates that NK-cell-derived IFN-γ drives the generation of mregDCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the increase of CCR7+LAMP3+ MHC-IIhi cDCs upon WT but not Ifng-/- NK cell transfer.

claim: Although Ifng-/- NK cells induced less cDC activation compared to WT NK cells, the levels of CD86 on cDCs of mice that received Ifng-/- NK cells were higher than those of mice not subjected to NK cell transfer.
source: However, although Ifng-/- NK cells induced less cDC activation compared to WT NK cells, the levels of CD86 on cDCs of mice that received Ifng-/- NK cells were higher than those of mice not subjected to NK cell transfer (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There are IFN-γ-independent or/and compensatory mechanism(s) for cDC activation by the transferred NK cells.
source: This outcome indicates the presence of IFN-γ-independent or/and compensatory mechanism(s) for cDC activation by the transferred NK cells, which is in line with our preliminary result that Ifng-/- NK cell therapy does not significantly diminish the pro-survival effect in comparison to WT NK cell therapy beyond 60 days after tumor cell inoculation (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the partial effect of Ifng-/- NK cells and preliminary survival data.

claim: IFN-γ is known to upregulate the expression of PD-L1.
source: IFN-γ is known to upregulate the expression of PD-L1 (Blank et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: IFN-γ of transferred NK cells augments the level of PD-L1 on cDCs, and the proportion of mregDCs that express the highest level of PD-L1 among lung cDC subsets.
source: Here, we found that IFN-γ of transferred NK cells augments the level of PD-L1 on cDCs, and the proportion of mregDCs that express the highest level of PD-L1 among lung cDC subsets (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4.

claim: PD-L1 is a ligand for the inhibitory PD-1 receptor that induces Treg cell expansion and inhibits CTL cytotoxicity.
source: PD-L1 is a ligand for the inhibitory PD-1 receptor that induces Treg cell expansion and inhibits CTL cytotoxicity (Arasanz et al., 2017; Dong et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PD-L1 on DCs inhibits T cell activation.
source: A previous study found that PD-L1 on DCs inhibits T cell activation (Peng et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Blockade of the PD-L1/PD-1 axis promotes activation of tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells that leads to tumor control.
source: Blockade of the PD-L1/PD-1 axis not only promotes activation of tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells that leads to tumor control, but also improves the number and functionality of SCL CD8+ T cells within tumors (Castiglioni et al., 2023; Peng et al., 2020; Siddiqui et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Blockade of the PD-L1/PD-1 axis improves the number and functionality of SCL CD8+ T cells within tumors.
source: Blockade of the PD-L1/PD-1 axis not only promotes activation of tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells that leads to tumor control, but also improves the number and functionality of SCL CD8+ T cells within tumors (Castiglioni et al., 2023; Peng et al., 2020; Siddiqui et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Transfer of NK cells isolated from the spleens of 7-week-old mice, combined with anti-PD-L1 treatment, restored the anti-tumor effect of anti-PD-L1 in aged mice of the MC38 tumor model.
source: Additionally, a recent study demonstrated that transfer of NK cells isolated from the spleens of 7-week-old mice, combined with anti-PD-L1 treatment, restored the anti-tumor effect of anti-PD-L1 in aged mice of the MC38 tumor model (Hou et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: A combination of adoptive NK cell therapy plus PD-L1 blockade could enhance the effectiveness of cancer treatments.
source: Collectively, we speculate that a combination of adoptive NK cell therapy plus PD-L1 blockade could enhance the effectiveness of cancer treatments.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the observed PD-L1 upregulation and prior literature on combination therapies.

claim: Syngeneic IL-15/IL-12-conditioned NK cell therapy promotes tumor-specific T cell responses, at least in part, through activation of cDC1s and cDC2s in metastatic lung.
source: In summary, our results indicate that syngeneic IL-15/IL-12-conditioned NK cell therapy promotes tumor-specific T cell responses, at least in part, through activation of cDC1s and cDC2s in metastatic lung.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: The findings are consistent with the critical role of endogenous NK cells and CD8+ T cells in anti-tumor immunity.
source: Our findings are consistent with the critical role of endogenous NK cells and CD8+ T cells in anti-tumor immunity, and support that autologous NK cell therapy is effective in treating established low burden MHC-I+ metastases by enhancing the tumor-specific CD8+ T cell response.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the consistency between the study findings and established knowledge.

claim: Autologous NK cell therapy is effective in treating established low burden MHC-I+ metastases by enhancing the tumor-specific CD8+ T cell response.
source: Our findings are consistent with the critical role of endogenous NK cells and CD8+ T cells in anti-tumor immunity, and support that autologous NK cell therapy is effective in treating established low burden MHC-I+ metastases by enhancing the tumor-specific CD8+ T cell response.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined mouse model and clinical trial data.

claim: Conventional DCs directly trigger an antigen-specific T cell response by providing ligands to antigen, costimulatory and cytokine receptors expressed on T cells.
source: Conventional DCs directly trigger an antigen-specific T cell response by providing ligands to antigen, costimulatory and cytokine receptors expressed on T cells (Cabeza-Cabrerizo, Cabeza-Cabrerizo et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: A20 lymphoma expressing abnormally low levels of MHC I molecules (MHC-I) induces IL-12 production by splenic DCs (CD11c+CD19-F4/80-) and CD8+ T cell response.
source: A previous in vivo study reported that A20 lymphoma expressing abnormally low levels of MHC I molecules (MHC-I) induces IL-12 production by splenic DCs (CD11c+CD19-F4/80-) and CD8+ T cell response (Mocikat et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: cDC1s and cDC2s present cell-associated and soluble antigens, respectively, to CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
source: cDC1s and cDC2s present cell-associated and soluble antigens, respectively, to CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Hildner et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: CCR7 mediates migration of cDC from tumor to its draining LN (dLN).
source: It is known that CCR7 mediates migration of cDC from tumor to its draining LN (dLN; Riol-Blanco et al., 2005), in which the migratory cDCs prime tumor-specific naive T cells (Mempel et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.
